raw_text:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a primary driver of ischemic stroke, with over 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF (NVAF) originating within the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. While oral anticoagulants (OACs), including direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), are the cornerstone of stroke prevention, a substantial cohort of patients face absolute or relative contraindications due to high bleeding risk [2,3]. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a landmark mechanical alternative to lifelong OAC therapy [4].

The clinical validation of percutaneous LAAC began with the PROTECT AF trial [5] and the subsequent PREVAIL trial [6], which randomized patients to the first-generation Watchman 2.5 device or warfarin. Long-term 5-year meta-analysis of these trials demonstrated that LAAC provided comparable stroke prevention to warfarin, with significant reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, and cardiovascular mortality [7,8]. For patients with absolute contraindications to OAC, the ASAP study demonstrated the safety and efficacy of implanting the Watchman device followed by dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) rather than transitional OAC [9]. This laid the groundwork for the ongoing ASAP-TOO trial evaluating LAAC in this vulnerable population [10].

As DOACs became the standard of care, the PRAGUE-17 trial directly compared LAAC (using both Watchman and Amulet devices) against DOAC therapy [11]. The 4-year follow-up of PRAGUE-17 confirmed that LAAC was non-inferior to DOACs regarding the composite endpoint of stroke, transient ischemic attack, clinically significant bleeding, or cardiovascular death [12]. Real-world registries, such as EWOLUTION [13,14] and the massive US National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) LAAO registry [15], have confirmed the high procedural success rate (>95%) and low complication rates of modern LAAC in clinical practice, even among high-risk patients like those with chronic kidney disease on dialysis [16]. Furthermore, the LAAOS III trial highlighted the prognostic benefits of surgical LAA exclusion, underscoring the pathophysiological importance of LAA management [17].

Technological advancements have dramatically refined LAAC safety. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug (ACP) [18] evolved into the Amplatzer Amulet, which utilizes a dual-component (lobe and disc) design. The Amulet IDE trial demonstrated that the Amulet was non-inferior to the Watchman 2.5, achieving higher rates of complete LAA occlusion [19]. Concurrently, the first-generation Watchman was succeeded by the Watchman FLX, designed with a closed-end distal contour and more anchors to improve safety and reduce leaks, as validated in the PINNACLE FLX trial [20]. Head-to-head comparison in the SWISS-APERO trial suggested that while both Amulet and Watchman FLX are highly effective, they exhibit distinct mechanical and sealing profiles [21]. Other innovative designs, such as the LAmbre device, offer tailor-made solutions for complex LAA anatomies [22].

Modern LAAC relies heavily on precise imaging. While transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and fluoroscopy remain standard, pre-procedural cardiac computed tomography (CT) angiography has become indispensable for 3D anatomical planning and device sizing [23]. Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) is also increasingly utilized as an alternative to TEE, minimizing the need for general anesthesia [24].

Despite excellent safety profiles, complications such as device-related thrombosis (DRT) and residual peridevice leaks (PDL) persist. DRT occurs in 2% to 4% of patients [25] and is associated with an elevated stroke risk; it is typically managed with transient anticoagulation [26]. Residual PDL, particularly those >5 mm, have traditionally been linked to worse outcomes [27], although recent data from large registries suggest even minor leaks require diligent monitoring and tailored antithrombotic regimens [28]. Post-LAAC antithrombotic strategies remain heterogeneous, varying from DAPT to short-term DOAC or single antiplatelet therapy, necessitating patient-specific decisions [29].

Finally, combining catheter ablation for AF and LAAC in a single-setting procedure has emerged as a feasible, safe, and cost-effective strategy to address both rhythm control and stroke prevention simultaneously [30].
